newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's first GDR may herald more issues, analysts.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's first GDR may herald more issues, analysts.

text.p: Jordan's first global depositary receipt (GDR) issue, to be issued by Arab Potash Company by year-end, will encourage major firms to tap equity markets for cheaper credit while raising the country's investor profile, investment bankers said on Tuesday.

"It will be a landmark deal, and the success of it will have two benefits, firstly major corporations will be encouraged by its success because it will be an alternate way to raise their capital and will give international investors a new look at Jordan," said Khaled al-Masri, investment manager at Arab Jordan Investment Bank (AJIB).

Arab Potash, the second largest capitalised firm in Jordan's stock market, took a groundbreaking step by inviting this week global banks to submit proposals on an estimated $50 million GDR listing it wants traded in international markets by year-end.

Masri, echoing the view of other bankers, said at least four other Jordanian publicly listed firms, both industrial and banks, would be watching this deal "to see if it proves to be an effective way to raise capital."

Amman Financial Market's (AFM) director general Wahib Shair said Jordanian firms mulling GDR proposals reflected heightened emerging fund interest in Jordan's bourse, which so far in the first half of 1997 has drawn unprecedented inflows.

Others like Ziad al-Basha, securities manager at Jordan's British Bank of the Middle East, said the GDR issue proves that the only viable venue for Jordanian companies to raise future capital was by tapping international markets.

Other potential candidates for a GDR listing which could follow in Arab Potash's steps are Jordan Cement Factories which is seeking funds for major industrial expansion projects, and larger banks such as Housing Bank and National Bank.

Investment managers expect tough competition by eight global investment banks invited by Arab Potash and given a one month deadline to submit details of their track record and pricing ranges, widely expected to be between 7 to 8 dinars ($11.29) per share.

"The sheer number of banks point to the fact that this issue will be hotly sought...being the first out of Jordan and the fact the number of GDRs which could emerge from the region are numbered," said another banker who requested anonymity.

Investment managers say the company has long been a focus of foreign investor interest, being one of Jordan's top exporters with a solid earnings record and ambitious downstream projects to exploit the reserves of the country's Dead Sea minerals.

The GDR will help foreign investors buy into a company with a limited 0.9 percent free float of tradeable stock on the Amman bourse, due to sizeable institutional and Arab government holdings on top of a majority 57 percent stake held by Jordan's government.

The GDR will offer 3.62 million shares left unsubscribed from a public float in 1994 to raise Arab Potash's capital to 83.3 million dinars, along with a portion of the government's stake in the firm's current 79.7 million dinars paid-up capital.
The GDR issue will help raise global funds ownership to four percent of the firm's capital from a minimal 0.9 percent currently owned by global emerging funds, company sources said.

Arab Potash's GDR issue comes at a time of growing foreign appetite for Jordan stocks and debt instruments. Two bonds issues expected to raise Jordan's emerging market profile are now in the pipeline: a $100 milion Eurobond issue by Jordan Phosphate Mines to be launched next month and a debut $70 million sovereign bond issue expected by year-end.
